The system organizes distinct records within a database environment that includes two separate database clusters: a first database cluster, referred to as cluster H, and a second database cluster, referred to as cluster L.

For each distinct record, the system determines a priority classification. In particular, the system identifies whether the record is a first-priority record or a second-priority record. This determination may be based on one or more criteria associated with the record, such as its importance, frequency of access, processing requirements, or relevance to system operations.

After the priority of each record is determined, the system stores the records according to their assigned priority. Records identified as first priority are stored in the first database cluster H. Records identified as second priority are stored in the second database cluster L.

The first database cluster H is implemented using a server having greater processing power than the server used by the second database cluster L. As a result, higher-priority records are maintained in a database cluster that is better suited for faster processing, higher performance, or more demanding workloads, while lower-priority records are maintained in a database cluster with comparatively lower processing capability.
outputs.L4:
A database system can organize and manage distinct records by classifying each record according to its assigned priority level. In this approach, incoming or existing records are evaluated to determine whether they should be treated as first-priority records or second-priority records. The classification may be based on one or more criteria, such as business importance, frequency of access, latency requirements, customer tier, transaction value, regulatory significance, or any other attribute that indicates how important the record is to the operation of the system.

After the priority level of a record has been determined, the database system stores the record in a corresponding database cluster. First-priority records are stored in a first database cluster, while second-priority records are stored in a separate second database cluster. By separating the records in this manner, the system can apply different resource configurations, performance policies, and management strategies to each group of data.

The first database cluster may be provisioned with greater computing power, faster storage, increased memory, higher network bandwidth, additional replication, or stronger availability guarantees. This enables the system to process higher-priority records more quickly and reliably. For example, records that are frequently queried or that support critical application functions can be placed in the more powerful cluster so that users experience reduced latency and improved responsiveness.

The second database cluster may be configured with fewer resources or a lower-cost infrastructure because it stores records that are less time-sensitive or less critical. These records remain available for processing and retrieval, but they do not consume the same level of system resources as the higher-priority records. As a result, the database system avoids over-provisioning all data equally and instead allocates resources where they provide the greatest benefit.

This priority-based grouping improves overall performance and resource efficiency. Important records receive faster access and stronger processing support, while lower-priority records are stored in a cluster that is appropriate for their operational requirements. The separation of records into different clusters also makes it easier to scale the system, adjust capacity, perform maintenance, and apply different backup or replication policies to different categories of data.

In practice, the database system may periodically reassess record priority. If a second-priority record becomes more important, it may be migrated to the first database cluster. Similarly, if a first-priority record becomes less critical over time, it may be moved to the second database cluster. This dynamic management allows the system to respond to changing workloads and business needs while maintaining efficient use of computing resources.

Overall, the described database system improves data management by grouping records according to priority and storing them in clusters that match their importance. By placing higher-priority records in a more powerful database cluster, the system enhances performance for critical data while reducing unnecessary resource consumption for less important records.

**Various and Other: The Value of Diversity in Everyday Life**

The words “various” and “other” may seem simple, but they represent an important idea: life is made up of many different people, places, experiences, and perspectives. Not everything fits neatly into one category. Some things are unique, mixed, unusual, or simply different from what we expect.

In everyday life, we encounter various choices, from the food we eat to the music we enjoy and the ways we communicate. These differences make the world more interesting and dynamic. If everything were the same, life would quickly become predictable and dull.

The word “other” often refers to something outside the usual group or category. It can describe alternative ideas, unfamiliar cultures, or different ways of thinking. Instead of ignoring what is “other,” we can learn from it. New experiences help us grow, become more open-minded, and understand the world better.

In business, education, art, and technology, variety is especially valuable. Different opinions can lead to better solutions. Other approaches can inspire innovation. Various skills and backgrounds can help teams solve problems more creatively.

Ultimately, “various” and “other” remind us that diversity matters. The world is not made of one single story, but of many stories connected together. By appreciating differences and staying open to new possibilities, we create a richer, more inclusive, and more meaningful life.

---

## Title

**Priority-Based Data Record Routing to Heterogeneous Database Clusters**

## Abstract

A system and method are provided for storing data records in different database clusters based on a priority classification of each record. A record classification component determines whether an incoming data record is associated with a high priority level or a low priority level. High priority records are routed to and stored in a first database cluster hosted on a relatively higher-performance server infrastructure. Low priority records are routed to and stored in a second database cluster hosted on a relatively lower-performance server infrastructure that is separate from the first database cluster. The arrangement enables computing resources to be allocated according to record importance, thereby improving performance for high priority data while reducing infrastructure cost for lower priority data.

## Field of the Invention

The present disclosure relates generally to data storage systems and, more particularly, to systems and methods for routing and storing records among multiple database clusters based on record priority.

## Background

Database systems commonly store records having different levels of importance, urgency, or performance sensitivity. Conventional systems may store all records in a common database cluster regardless of their relative priority. As a result, expensive high-performance infrastructure may be used for records that do not require such resources, or lower-priority records may compete for resources with records requiring faster access, higher reliability, or greater processing capacity.

There is therefore a need for a storage architecture that assigns records to different database resources based on priority, so that higher-priority records may be stored on stronger computing infrastructure while lower-priority records may be stored on less costly infrastructure.

## Summary

In one embodiment, a computer-implemented method includes receiving a data record, determining a priority classification associated with the data record, and routing the data record to one of a plurality of database clusters based on the priority classification. If the data record is classified as high priority, the data record is stored in a first database cluster hosted on a first server or server group having relatively greater processing, memory, storage, network, or availability resources. If the data record is classified as low priority, the data record is stored in a second database cluster hosted on a second server or server group having relatively lesser computing resources than the first server or server group.

In another embodiment, a system includes a record intake module, a priority classification module, a routing module, a high priority database cluster, and a low priority database cluster. The routing module directs high priority records to the high priority database cluster and directs low priority records to the low priority database cluster.

## Detailed Description

In various embodiments, a data storage system receives data records from one or more client applications, services, sensors, user interfaces, transaction systems, or other data sources. Each received record is evaluated to determine a priority classification. The priority classification may be determined from metadata included with the record, a field value contained in the record, a source identity, a user account type, a transaction type, a service-level agreement, a rule set, a machine learning model, or any combination thereof.

The system may classify each record into at least two priority classes, including a high priority class and a low priority class. In some embodiments, additional intermediate priority classes may also be supported, but the system includes at least a distinction between high priority records and low priority records.

A routing component selects a destination database cluster based on the determined priority classification. Records classified as high priority are transmitted to a first database cluster, referred to herein as cluster H. Cluster H is implemented using a first computing infrastructure having higher performance characteristics. For example, cluster H may be hosted on one or more servers having faster processors, larger memory capacity, faster storage devices, greater input/output throughput, higher network bandwidth, increased redundancy, or enhanced availability relative to a second computing infrastructure.

Records classified as low priority are transmitted to a second database cluster, referred to herein as cluster L. Cluster L is implemented using a second computing infrastructure different from the first computing infrastructure. The second computing infrastructure may have lower performance characteristics than the first computing infrastructure and may be selected to reduce cost while still providing adequate storage and access capabilities for low priority records.

In an embodiment, cluster H and cluster L are physically or logically separate database clusters. The clusters may be implemented using the same database engine or different database engines. The routing component may maintain connection information for each cluster and may write each incoming record to the appropriate cluster based on the record’s classification.

In certain embodiments, the classification module assigns a priority value to a record before storage. The assigned priority value may be stored together with the record, stored in an index or metadata table, or used only during routing. The system may also log routing decisions for audit, monitoring, troubleshooting, or compliance purposes.

The system may further include a policy management interface by which an administrator defines rules for classifying records. For example, records associated with payment processing, security events, emergency alerts, premium users, or time-sensitive transactions may be classified as high priority. Records associated with archival information, batch reports, diagnostic logs, noncritical analytics, or background events may be classified as low priority.

In some embodiments, records may be reclassified after initial storage. A record initially stored in cluster L may be migrated to cluster H if its priority increases. Conversely, a record initially stored in cluster H may be migrated to cluster L if its priority decreases or after a retention period expires. Such migration may be performed by a background process while preserving record identifiers or maintaining a mapping table indicating the current location of each record.

By separating high priority and low priority records into different database clusters hosted on servers of different capability, the disclosed system can allocate high-performance resources to records most likely to require them while reducing the burden placed on high-performance infrastructure by lower-priority records.

## Example Claim Set

### Claim 1

A computer-implemented method comprising:

receiving, by one or more processors, a data record;

determining, by the one or more processors, a priority classification of the data record, the priority classification comprising at least one of a high priority classification and a low priority classification;

in response to determining that the data record has the high priority classification, routing the data record to a first database cluster hosted on a first server infrastructure; and

in response to determining that the data record has the low priority classification, routing the data record to a second database cluster hosted on a second server infrastructure different from the first server infrastructure;

wherein the first server infrastructure has greater computing resources than the second server infrastructure.

### Claim 2

The computer-implemented method of claim 1, wherein the greater computing resources comprise at least one of greater processor capacity, greater memory capacity, faster storage, greater input/output throughput, greater network bandwidth, or greater availability.

### Claim 3

The computer-implemented method of claim 1, wherein determining the priority classification comprises evaluating metadata associated with the data record.

### Claim 4

The computer-implemented method of claim 1, wherein determining the priority classification comprises applying one or more administrator-defined classification rules.

### Claim 5

The computer-implemented method of claim 1, further comprising storing an indication of the priority classification in association with the data record.

### Claim 6

The computer-implemented method of claim 1, further comprising logging a routing decision identifying whether the data record was routed to the first database cluster or the second database cluster.

### Claim 7

The computer-implemented method of claim 1, further comprising migrating a stored data record from the second database cluster to the first database cluster in response to a change in priority classification.

### Claim 8

A data storage system comprising:

a record intake module configured to receive data records;

a priority classification module configured to classify each received data record as at least one of high priority or low priority;

a routing module configured to route high priority data records to a first database cluster and low priority data records to a second database cluster;

the first database cluster being hosted on a first server infrastructure; and

the second database cluster being hosted on a second server infrastructure different from the first server infrastructure;

wherein the first server infrastructure has greater computing resources than the second server infrastructure.

### Claim 9

The data storage system of claim 8, wherein the first database cluster and the second database cluster are logically separate clusters.

### Claim 10

The data storage system of claim 8, wherein the first database cluster and the second database cluster are physically separate clusters.

### Claim 11

The data storage system of claim 8, further comprising a policy management interface configured to receive classification rules used by the priority classification module.

### Claim 12

A non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by one or more processors, cause the one or more processors to:

receive a data record;

determine whether the data record is high priority or low priority;

store the data record in a high priority database cluster when the data record is determined to be high priority; and

store the data record in a low priority database cluster when the data record is determined to be low priority;

wherein the high priority database cluster is hosted on computing infrastructure having greater performance capability than computing infrastructure hosting the low priority database cluster.

counterfactuals.output:
### Example Embodiment: Priority-Based Grouping of Distinct Database Records Across Clusters

In one embodiment, a computer-implemented system is configured to group distinct database records distributed across a first database cluster, referred to herein as cluster **H**, and a second database cluster, referred to herein as cluster **L**, according to at least a first priority level and a second priority level. Cluster H and cluster L may each include one or more database nodes, partitions, shards, replicas, tables, indexes, or other logical or physical storage resources. The records stored in cluster H and cluster L may include structured, semi-structured, or unstructured data, and may be uniquely identifiable by one or more record identifiers, keys, hashes, timestamps, metadata fields, or combinations thereof.

In some embodiments, the system receives or accesses a plurality of database records from cluster H and a plurality of database records from cluster L. The system determines whether records from the respective clusters are distinct based on one or more distinctness criteria. Such criteria may include, for example, a unique record identifier, a primary key, a composite key, a checksum, a hash value, a version identifier, a timestamp, a semantic similarity score, or any combination thereof. Records determined to be duplicates or non-distinct may be filtered, merged, flagged, or otherwise processed before priority-based grouping is performed.

The system assigns each distinct record to one of a plurality of priority levels, including at least a first priority level and a second priority level. In one embodiment, the first priority level corresponds to records having a higher processing precedence than records assigned to the second priority level. Priority assignment may be based on one or more priority attributes, including without limitation record source, cluster origin, record age, transaction value, service-level requirement, access frequency, error state, dependency status, user designation, system policy, security classification, or a computed priority score.

In certain embodiments, records associated with cluster H are initially assigned to the first priority level and records associated with cluster L are initially assigned to the second priority level. In other embodiments, the designation of clusters H and L does not itself determine priority; rather, records from either cluster may be assigned to either the first priority level or the second priority level based on the applicable priority attributes. For example, a record from cluster L may be promoted to the first priority level when it satisfies a high-priority condition, and a record from cluster H may be demoted to the second priority level when it fails to satisfy such a condition.

After assigning priority levels, the system groups the distinct records into a first group corresponding to the first priority level and a second group corresponding to the second priority level. Each group may include records from cluster H, cluster L, or both. The grouping may be stored in memory, written to a database table, represented as an index, maintained as a queue, exposed through an application programming interface, or used to control downstream processing. In some implementations, the first group is processed before the second group, allocated additional computational resources, replicated with higher urgency, subjected to enhanced validation, or transmitted to a downstream service ahead of the second group.

In one embodiment, the system performs the grouping by executing instructions that cause one or more processors to: obtain a first set of database records from cluster H; obtain a second set of database records from cluster L; identify distinct records among the first and second sets; determine a priority level for each distinct record according to a priority rule set; generate a first priority group including records assigned to the first priority level; generate a second priority group including records assigned to the second priority level; and store, output, or otherwise make available the first and second priority groups.

The priority rule set may include static rules, dynamic rules, machine-learned scoring models, threshold comparisons, user-defined policies, administrative configuration data, or combinations thereof. In some embodiments, the priority rule set is updated periodically or in response to detected system conditions, such as cluster load, latency, replication lag, record volume, failure events, or changes in business requirements.

In further embodiments, the grouping process includes resolving conflicts between records from cluster H and cluster L. For example, where two records correspond to a common entity but differ in one or more field values, the system may select a representative record, merge fields, preserve multiple versions, or assign the records to different priority groups based on a conflict-resolution policy. The conflict-resolution policy may take into account cluster origin, recency, trust level, validation status, or priority score.

The described priority-based grouping may be implemented in hardware, software, firmware, or any combination thereof. For example, the operations may be performed by a server, distributed processing system, database management system, middleware layer, data synchronization engine, message broker, or cloud-based computing environment. Instructions for performing the operations may be stored on a non-transitory computer-readable medium and executed by one or more processors.

Although certain examples describe two clusters, H and L, and two priority levels, the disclosure is not limited to such examples. Additional clusters, additional priority levels, nested groups, sub-priorities, or alternative grouping criteria may be used without departing from the scope of the disclosed embodiment. Similarly, the labels “H” and “L” are used for convenience and do not necessarily require that cluster H be of higher priority than cluster L unless expressly specified by a particular implementation.
